expectedText:
CALIFORNIA "ERASER LAW" (MINOR'S RIGHT TO REMOVE POSTED CONTENT) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc. · https://www.acme.com

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's "Eraser Law," Business and Professions Code sections 22580 through 22582 (the "Privacy Rights for California Minors in the Digital World Act") — a state statute requiring an operator of an Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application directed to minors, or that has actual knowledge a minor is using it, to permit a minor who is a registered user to remove, or request and obtain removal of, content or information the minor themselves posted. It states facts about who the statute covers, the removal right's precise scope, the notice the statute requires, and the statute's own exceptions and safe harbor, as those may relate to Acme, Inc.'s online service, product, or feature located at https://www.acme.com. This information sheet does not itself determine whether Acme, Inc.'s Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application is "directed to minors" or whether Acme, Inc. has "actual knowledge" a minor is using it, does not constitute the notice or instructions the statute requires an operator to provide, and does not tell Acme, Inc. what to do about any specific removal request, design feature, or practice.

COVERAGE TRIGGER: "DIRECTED TO MINORS" OR "ACTUAL KNOWLEDGE," AND THE STATUTE'S OWN DEFINITIONS
The Eraser Law's removal-right duties apply to an operator under either of two independent triggers, joined by "or": an operator whose Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application is directed to minors, or an operator that has actual knowledge that a minor is using its Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application — the duty is not limited to sites built for minors, and reaches an operator of a general-audience site once it has actual knowledge a minor is a user. The statute defines "directed to minors," for this chapter, itself: an Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application, or a portion of one, created for the purpose of reaching an audience predominately comprised of minors and not intended for a more general adult audience. Separately, this chapter defines "minor" to mean a natural person under 18 years of age who resides in California, and defines "operator" to mean any person or entity that owns the Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application — expressly excluding a third party that merely operates, hosts, or manages it, or processes information, on the owner's behalf.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "An operator of an Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application directed to minors or an operator of an Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application that has actual knowledge that a minor is using its Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application shall do all of the following:"
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22581(a) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), Eraser Law, dual coverage trigger: directed to minors, or actual knowledge a minor is a user (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=22581.)
  "“Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application directed to minors” mean an Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application, or a portion thereof, that is created for the purpose of reaching an audience that is predominately comprised of minors, and is not intended for a more general audience comprised of adults."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22580(e) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), Eraser Law chapter, definition of "directed to minors" (self-contained, no COPPA cross-reference) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=22580.)
  "“Minor” means a natural person under 18 years of age who resides in this state."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22580(d) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), Eraser Law chapter, definition of "minor" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=22580.)
  "“Operator” means any person or entity that owns an Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application. It does not include any third party that operates, hosts, or manages, but does not own, an Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application on the owner’s behalf or processes information on the owner’s behalf."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22580(f) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), Eraser Law chapter, definition of "operator" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=22580.)
  Known gap: The first citation below is to Business and Professions Code section 22581(a), the operative removal-right section; the remaining three citations are to section 22580(d), (e), and (f) — three subsections of the same statutory section as one another — they are not independent of one another. Section 22580 is a genuinely separate, independently numbered section from section 22581, so the first citation is independent of the other three. Section 22581 does not itself restate these definitions; this clause treats section 22580's definitions of "directed to minors," "minor," and "operator" as governing section 22581 because both sections appear in the same chapter (Chapter 22.1, sections 22580 through 22582) and section 22581 uses the identical defined terms without supplying its own definitions — that is an ordinary statutory-construction reading, not text quoted from section 22581 itself, and no case law was checked confirming that a court has applied section 22580's definitions to section 22581 specifically. On the statute's own text quoted below, the "directed to minors" definition is self-contained and does not cross-reference the federal Children's Online Privacy Protection Act or any other statute's definition — this is a real difference from California's Age-Appropriate Design Code Act, whose separate "likely to be accessed by children" coverage test (documented elsewhere in this corpus) does cross-reference COPPA as one of several indicators. This clause does not determine whether any specific Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application is in fact "directed to minors" or whether a specific operator in fact has "actual knowledge" a minor is using it — those are fact-specific determinations this document does not make.

THE CORE REMOVAL RIGHT IS LIMITED TO CONTENT THE MINOR REGISTERED USER POSTED THEMSELVES
Business and Professions Code section 22581(a)(1) requires a covered operator to permit a minor who is a registered user to remove, or, if the operator prefers instead, to request and obtain removal of, content or information posted on the operator's Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application by that same user. The statute gives the operator a choice of mechanism — direct self-service removal, or a request-and-obtain-removal process — but either way the right runs only to content or information the registered minor user posted. This is not a general right for a minor, or anyone on the minor's behalf, to have all content about the minor taken down: section 22581(b)(2) expressly carves out of the removal duty any content or information that was stored on or posted to the operator's service by a third party other than the minor registered user, including content the minor posted that a third party then stored, republished, or reposted. "Posted," as the statute itself defines the term, means content or information that can be accessed by a user in addition to the minor who posted it, whether that other user is a registered user of the service or not.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "Permit a minor who is a registered user of the operator’s Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application to remove or, if the operator prefers, to request and obtain removal of, content or information posted on the operator’s Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application by the user."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22581(a)(1) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), Eraser Law, core removal right for a minor registered user's own posted content (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=22581.)
  "The content or information was stored on or posted to the operator’s Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application by a third party other than the minor, who is a registered user, including any content or information posted by the registered user that was stored, republished, or reposted by the third party."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22581(b)(2) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), Eraser Law, exception for content posted by a third party rather than the minor registered user (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=22581.)
  "“Posted” means content or information that can be accessed by a user in addition to the minor who posted the content or information, whether the user is a registered user or not, of the Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application where the content or information is posted."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22581(f) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), Eraser Law, definition of "posted" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=22581.)
  Known gap: All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section, Business and Professions Code § 22581 — subdivision (a)(1) (the removal right itself), subdivision (b)(2) (the third-party-posted-content exception), and subdivision (f) (the definition of "posted") — they are not independent of one another. This clause does not address the notice and instructions the operator must separately provide about this right, covered in a companion clause, or the statute's remaining exceptions and its "deemed compliant" safe harbor for making content invisible rather than deleting it, also covered in a companion clause. This clause does not determine, for any specific piece of content, whether it was in fact posted by the minor registered user themselves or by a third party — that is a fact-specific determination this document does not make.

NOTICE AND INSTRUCTIONS THE OPERATOR MUST PROVIDE TO A MINOR REGISTERED USER
Beyond the removal right itself, Business and Professions Code section 22581(a) requires a covered operator to take three further, related actions. The operator must provide notice to a minor registered user that the minor may remove, or, if the operator prefers, request and obtain removal of, content or information the minor posted. The operator must also provide clear instructions to the minor registered user on how to do so. Finally, the operator must provide notice to the minor registered user that this removal does not ensure complete or comprehensive removal of the posted content or information — the statute itself requires the operator to disclose the limits of what removal will accomplish, rather than allowing the notice to imply the content will be permanently or completely gone.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "Provide notice to a minor who is a registered user of the operator’s Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application that the minor may remove or, if the operator prefers, request and obtain removal of, content or information posted on the operator’s Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application by the registered user."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22581(a)(2) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), Eraser Law, duty to notify a minor registered user of the removal right (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=22581.)
  "Provide clear instructions to a minor who is a registered user of the operator’s Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application on how the user may remove or, if the operator prefers, request and obtain the removal of content or information posted on the operator’s Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22581(a)(3) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), Eraser Law, duty to provide clear instructions on how to remove or request removal (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=22581.)
  "Provide notice to a minor who is a registered user of the operator’s Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application that the removal described under paragraph (1) does not ensure complete or comprehensive removal of the content or information posted on the operator’s Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application by the registered user."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22581(a)(4) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), Eraser Law, duty to disclose that removal does not ensure complete or comprehensive removal (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=22581.)
  Known gap: All three citations below are paragraphs of the same subdivision of the same statutory section, Business and Professions Code § 22581(a) — paragraphs (2), (3), and (4) — they are not independent of one another, and are also not independent of paragraph (1) (the removal right itself), quoted in a companion clause of this document. This clause does not address the statute's exceptions to the underlying removal duty or its "deemed compliant" safe harbor, both covered in a companion clause; a notice given under this clause's requirements can be accurate about the limits of removal precisely because those exceptions and the safe harbor exist. This clause does not specify the notice's required format, placement, or delivery method beyond what the statute's own text requires, and does not determine whether any specific operator's actual notice or instructions in fact satisfy this standard — that is a fact-specific determination this document does not make.

THE STATUTE'S OWN EXCEPTIONS, AND ITS "DEEMED COMPLIANT" SAFE HARBOR: INVISIBILITY, NOT GUARANTEED DELETION
Business and Professions Code section 22581(b) lists five circumstances in which an operator or a third party is not required to erase or otherwise eliminate, or to enable erasure or elimination of, content or information: where another provision of federal or state law requires the operator or third party to maintain it; where the content was stored or posted by a third party other than the minor registered user (including the minor's own content that a third party stored, republished, or reposted); where the operator anonymizes the content so the minor registered user cannot be individually identified; where the minor fails to follow the removal instructions the operator provided; and where the minor received compensation or other consideration for providing the content. Separately, section 22581(d) states what an operator must actually do to satisfy this section: an operator is deemed compliant if it renders the minor user's posted content or information no longer visible to other users of the service and to the public, even if the content or information remains on the operator's servers in some form — the statute requires inaccessibility to others, not guaranteed deletion from the operator's systems. The same subdivision further provides that an operator remains deemed compliant even if the content stays visible because a third party copied or reposted it, so long as the operator made the minor's original posting invisible.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "An operator or a third party is not required to erase or otherwise eliminate, or to enable erasure or elimination of, content or information in any of the following circumstances: (1) Any other provision of federal or state law requires the operator or third party to maintain the content or information. (2) The content or information was stored on or posted to the operator’s Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application by a third party other than the minor, who is a registered user, including any content or information posted by the registered user that was stored, republished, or reposted by the third party. (3) The operator anonymizes the content or information posted by the minor who is a registered user, so that the minor who is a registered user cannot be individually identified. (4) The minor does not follow the instructions provided to the minor pursuant to paragraph (3) of subdivision (a) on how the registered user may request and obtain the removal of content or information posted on the operator’s Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application by the registered user. (5) The minor has received compensation or other consideration for providing the content."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22581(b) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), Eraser Law, the statute's own five exceptions to the removal duty (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=22581.)
  "An operator shall be deemed compliant with this section if: (1) It renders the content or information posted by the minor user no longer visible to other users of the service and the public even if the content or information remains on the operator’s servers in some form. (2) Despite making the original posting by the minor user invisible, it remains visible because a third party has copied the posting or reposted the content or information posted by the minor."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22581(d) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), Eraser Law, "deemed compliant" safe harbor: invisibility to others, not guaranteed deletion (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=22581.)
  Known gap: Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section, Business and Professions Code § 22581 — subdivision (b) and subdivision (d) — they are not independent of one another, and neither is independent of the removal right, notice duties, or "posted"/third-party-content provisions of the same section quoted in companion clauses of this document. This clause does not quote section 22581(c), which states that this section is not to be construed to limit a law enforcement agency's authority to obtain content or information from an operator as otherwise authorized by law or court order, or section 22581(e), which, like the coverage-trigger provisions addressed in a companion clause, states that the section does not require an operator to collect age information about users — both were reviewed in the same fetched section but are not separately quoted here. This clause states the statute's own text defining what counts as compliance; it does not determine, for any specific operator's specific technical implementation, whether content has in fact been rendered no longer visible to other users and the public, or whether a specific circumstance in fact falls within one of the five listed exceptions — those are fact-specific determinations this document does not make.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22581(d) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: Eraser Law, "deemed compliant" safe harbor: invisibility to others, not guaranteed deletion
citations.quote: An operator shall be deemed compliant with this section if: (1) It renders the content or information posted by the minor user no longer visible to other users of the service and the public even if the content or information remains on the operator’s servers in some form. (2) Despite making the original posting by the minor user invisible, it remains visible because a third party has copied the posting or reposted the content or information posted by the minor.

expectedJSON.gap: Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section, Business and Professions Code § 22581 — subdivision (b) and subdivision (d) — they are not independent of one another, and neither is independent of the removal right, notice duties, or "posted"/third-party-content provisions of the same section quoted in companion clauses of this document. This clause does not quote section 22581(c), which states that this section is not to be construed to limit a law enforcement agency's authority to obtain content or information from an operator as otherwise authorized by law or court order, or section 22581(e), which, like the coverage-trigger provisions addressed in a companion clause, states that the section does not require an operator to collect age information about users — both were reviewed in the same fetched section but are not separately quoted here. This clause states the statute's own text defining what counts as compliance; it does not determine, for any specific operator's specific technical implementation, whether content has in fact been rendered no longer visible to other users and the public, or whether a specific circumstance in fact falls within one of the five listed exceptions — those are fact-specific determinations this document does not make.
